script.opening: “My granddaughter made me do this. It’s only a little spot on my nose that bleeds when I wash my face. I just want a cream for it. I can’t be going up the hospital, I look after my husband.”

facts.text: About 18 months. Started like a pimple, very slowly bigger, now “the size of a pea”. Shiny, pearly edge, tiny red veins, a crust in the middle that bleeds when she washes, scabs, then breaks again. Not painful. No other spots like it.
Fair skin, freckles. Worked on her parents’ farm as a girl, “always out in the sun, no such thing as sun cream”. No previous skin cancers. No weight loss, no lumps in the neck.

Cares for Ted, 85, with vascular dementia, who wanders and cannot be left alone for long. Daughter lives 200 miles away; granddaughter visits on Sundays. No paid carers. Has never had a carer’s assessment.

facts.topic: Only if asked what worries her
facts.text: Her sister Joan had skin cancer on her nose 20 years ago and “they cut half of it off”. Joan stopped going out and never got over it. Peggy has avoided getting this looked at for that reason.
Hypertension on amlodipine. Mobile, independent, drives locally. Tired from caring.

Matter-of-fact and dismissive at first: “At my age, what does it matter?” Becomes emotional describing Joan. Engages if the doctor explains that this type rarely spreads, that treatment now is smaller and better than it was, and offers help with Ted for the appointment.

ice.ideas: “It’s a sore that won’t heal because I keep knocking it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: fear of disfigurement after her sister’s experience; also worry about who would look after Ted.

cues: “My granddaughter made me do this” — someone is worried; why hasn’t she come sooner?
Bleeding, crusting and never fully healing for 18 months — a lesion that needs referral.
“I look after my husband” — a carer with practical barriers and no support.
Emotion when talking about her sister — the hidden fear.

checkpoints.text: Takes a lesion history (duration, growth, bleeding, healing, symptoms) and risk factors (sun exposure, skin type, previous skin cancer), and examines the photos and on camera (pearly rolled edge, telangiectasia, central crust or ulceration)

Reaches a working diagnosis of probable basal cell carcinoma and considers the differential (squamous cell carcinoma, keratoacanthoma, amelanotic melanoma), checking for features that would change urgency

Applies NICE NG12 correctly: routine referral for suspected BCC, considering a suspected cancer pathway only if delay could have a significant impact because of site or size, and following local pathways for facial lesions; does not prescribe a cream
Explains the diagnosis honestly: a skin cancer that grows slowly and very rarely spreads, but is best treated while small, especially on the nose
Explores her reluctance and uncovers the fear of disfigurement based on her sister’s experience

Addresses the fear with accurate information about current treatment options (surgery with reconstruction, Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk facial sites, radiotherapy or other options), decided with the specialist
Solves practical barriers: cover for Ted on the day (family, respite or sitting services), hospital transport if eligible, and a referral for a Carer’s Assessment (Care Act 2014)
Respects her right to decide, agrees a plan she accepts, and safety-nets (rapid growth, pain, a new lump, a new lesion, or the appointment not arriving)

worked.txt: “From the photos, this looks like a basal cell carcinoma. It’s a type of skin cancer, but it’s the gentlest kind: it grows slowly and very rarely spreads to other parts of the body.”
“If it’s left, it keeps slowly growing into the skin around it. On the nose, smaller is much easier to treat, with a smaller scar.”
“You’ve had this a while. Has something made you wary of getting it looked at?”

“That sounds awful for Joan and for you. Things have changed a lot in 20 years. For spots on the nose there’s a special technique that removes only the affected skin, checking under the microscope as they go, to keep as much healthy skin as possible.”

“Let’s work out how you’d get there. Could your granddaughter sit with Ted on the day? If not, there are sitting services, and I’d like to refer you for a carer’s assessment so you get some support anyway.”
“It’s your decision. What I’d suggest is a referral to the skin specialists so you can hear the options. You can decide once you know what they’d do.”

f.learning: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the commonest skin cancer, typically on sun-exposed skin of the head and neck in older people. It presents as a slowly enlarging, pearly or translucent nodule with a rolled edge and telangiectasia, often with central ulceration or crusting that bleeds and fails to heal. It grows locally and can destroy surrounding tissue, but metastasis is very rare. NICE NG12 recommends considering routine referral for a skin lesion that raises suspicion of BCC, and considering a suspected cancer pathway referral only if there is particular concern that a delay may have a significant impact because of factors such as lesion site or size; facial lesions near the eyes, nose and lips are high-risk sites for recurrence and are often handled through local pathways. GPs should not treat suspected facial BCCs with creams or minor surgery outside accredited arrangements. Specialist treatment options include surgical excision, Mohs micrographic surgery (tissue-sparing, used for high-risk facial sites and recurrent tumours), radiotherapy for some older patients, and topical treatments or curettage for selected low-risk superficial lesions. The contrast with the related case of a suspected squamous cell carcinoma is important: SCC is faster-growing, often tender and can metastasise, so NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral. The consultation challenge here is an older carer who minimises the lesion because of fear of disfigurement from a family experience and because she cannot leave her husband. Honest, proportionate information, addressing the specific fear, practical help with caring responsibilities (respite, transport, a Carer’s Assessment under the Care Act 2014), and respect for her autonomy lead to a plan she can accept.

model.text: Hello Mrs Lowe, I’m Dr Clarke. I’ve got your photos here. What would you like help with?
Call me Peggy. My granddaughter made me do this. It’s only a little spot on my nose that bleeds when I wash. I just want a cream. I can’t be going up the hospital, I look after my husband.
Thanks, Peggy. I’ll keep in mind that you’re looking after your husband. Tell me about the spot. How long has it been there?
About a year and a half. Started like a pimple. Very slowly bigger. It scabs, bleeds when I wash, then scabs again.
Has it ever fully healed? Is it painful? Any other spots like it, or lumps in your neck?
Never properly healed. Doesn’t hurt. No other ones.
Did you spend a lot of time in the sun when you were younger? Any skin cancers before?
On the farm as a girl, always outside. Never had anything like this.

Could you hold your face close to the camera in good light? Thank you. I can see a shiny, pearly lump about the size of a pea with a raised edge, tiny blood vessels and a crust in the middle. That matches your photos.
Peggy, I’d like to be honest with you. This looks like a basal cell carcinoma. It’s a type of skin cancer, but the gentlest kind. It grows slowly and very rarely spreads elsewhere in the body.
Cancer. I thought it might be. At my age, what does it matter?
It does matter, because left alone it keeps slowly growing into the skin around it, and on the nose a smaller one is much easier to treat. A cream won’t treat this kind of spot.
You’ve had this a while. Has something made you wary of getting it looked at?
(tearful) My sister Joan. They cut half her nose off for skin cancer. She never went out again. I couldn’t bear that.

That sounds awful, for Joan and for you. Thank you for telling me. Things have changed a lot. For spots on the nose, there’s a technique where they remove only the affected skin, checking under the microscope as they go, to keep as much healthy skin as possible. Smaller spots also mean smaller repairs. The specialist would talk through all the options with you, including ones that aren’t surgery.
I didn’t know that.

What I’d suggest is a referral to the skin specialists. This type isn’t one where we need to rush, but because it’s on your nose I’ll send it through the pathway for face lesions so it’s seen by the right team. You can hear the options and decide then.
model.why: NG12 routine referral; local facial pathway

model.text: But Ted. I can’t leave him.

Let’s solve that. Could your granddaughter sit with him on the day? If not, there are sitting services and short respite stays. I can check if you’re eligible for hospital transport. And I’d like to refer you for a carer’s assessment, so you get some support with Ted anyway. You’re doing a lot on your own.
Sundays she comes. She’d do it if it was a weekday, I think. A carer’s assessment would be nice.
Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
It’s the slow kind of skin cancer. You’ll refer me, they might not need to cut much. You’ll sort a carer’s assessment and I’ll ask my granddaughter.

Exactly. Keep it clean with a little Vaseline and cover it if it bleeds. If it grows quickly, becomes painful, you notice a lump in your neck or a new spot, or you haven’t heard about the appointment in eight weeks, let me know.

social.t: Older carers frequently delay their own care because they cannot leave the person they care for. Practical solutions make attendance possible.
A relative’s bad experience often shapes how people imagine treatment. Ask about it.

legal.t: Under the Care Act 2014, carers in England are entitled to an assessment of their needs by the local authority.
She can decline referral after understanding the risks and options; document and offer review (GMC Decision making and consent).

professional.t: Using NG12 correctly (routine for BCC, suspected cancer pathway for SCC and melanoma) protects capacity for urgent cases and avoids unnecessary alarm.
Naming cancer honestly, with proportion, supports informed decisions.

community.t: Local carers’ centres, sitting services and respite care can provide cover for appointments.
Available for eligible patients, according to local criteria.
